newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs ask Vatican to help Croatian Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs ask Vatican to help Croatian Serbs.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs asked the Vatican on Thursday to help ensure that the human rights of Serbs in Croatia are protected when a breakaway enclave there returns to Croatian government rule in mid-1997.

The appeal was surprising because Orthodox Serbs in both Bosnia and Croatia have long been hostile to the Vatican over its alleged support for Catholic Croats and Bosnian Moslems in wars that shattered both countries in 1991-95.
Pope John Paul had to call off a planned visit to Sarajevo in September 1994 after Bosnian Serbs besieging the Bosnian capital at the time refused to guarantee his safety.
But the Vatican said on Thursday the Pope would finally visit Sarajevo, now at peace, on April 13.

SRNA, the Bosnian Serb news agency, said Momcilo Krajisnik, nationalist Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, met Papal Nuncio Monsignor Francesco Monterisi in Pale and asked the Holy See to intervene with the Croatian government over the future of Serbs in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia.

Krajisnik wanted the Vatican to help prevent an exodus of Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and protect Serb rights there once transitional U.N. administrators turn the area back to Croatian rule after five years as a separatist entity carved out in war.
It was not known whether Krajisnik's meeting with the papal nuncio was held before or after the Vatican's announcement that the pope would go to Sarajevo.

SRNA said Krajisnik also told Monterisi that, by accepting the role of mediator in Eastern Slavonia, the Holy See would help repair damaged trust between Orthodox and Catholic communities in the entire region of former Yugoslavia.
About 120,000 Serbs, half of them refugees from former war zones elsewhere in Croatia, live in Eastern Slavonia.
Analysts say many Serbs are so fearful and distrustful of incoming Croatian authorities that they may flee to nearby Serb-controlled Bosnia, if not to Serbia.

Krajisnik told Monterisi that if Serbs were guaranteed the right to a single provincial district and autonomy and allowed special ties with Serbs in the Bosnian Serb republic and Serbia, they would not need to leave Eastern Slavonia.

Croatia and the United Nations have repeatedly ruled out Serb demands for self-rule in Eastern Slavonia but say the Serbs will enjoy cultural and education rights and be treated the same as other Croatian citizens.

In rejecting autonomy, they have noted that Eastern Slavonia falls within Croatia's U.N.-recognised borders, that Serbs signed an agreement for complete reintegration in Croatia and that the area had a Croatian majority before 1991.

Virtually all Eastern Slavonia's 100,000-odd Croats fled or were expelled by Serb rebels who seized the region during Croatia's 1991 war for independence from federal Yugoslavia, which now comprises only Serbia and Montenegro.
